questions.q: How does the editorial describe intolerance?
options: As differences of opinion that have not been managed
Yes. Managed, they lead to development; unmanaged, to breakdown.
As a problem peculiar to one country
Not quite. The article says: As differences of opinion that have not been managed.
As the natural end of every disagreement
Not quite. The article says: As differences of opinion that have not been managed.
As something only governments can cure
Not quite. The article says: As differences of opinion that have not been managed.
questions.rationale: “Intolerance is only an improper name for differences of opinion… In truth, intolerance is a phenomenon of unmanaged differences.”

questions.q: What does the editorial ask of those who want to do something about intolerance?
options: To withdraw from public life
Not quite. The article says: To educate people in the value of tolerance, not merely protest about it.
To answer intolerance in kind
Not quite. The article says: To educate people in the value of tolerance, not merely protest about it.
To demand new laws
Not quite. The article says: To educate people in the value of tolerance, not merely protest about it.
To educate people in the value of tolerance, not merely protest about it
Right. Talking alone is an escape from duty.
questions.rationale: “Those who want to do something about the issue of intolerance must not protest against it in speech or writing, but educate the masses.”

questions.q: “If you run after two hares, you will catch neither.” What kind of mind does the article say achievement requires?
options: A single-focused mind fixed on one goal
Yes. A divided mind becomes “Jack-of-all, Master of none.”
A mind that changes goals often
Not quite. The article says: A single-focused mind fixed on one goal.
A mind busy with many projects at once
Not quite. The article says: A single-focused mind fixed on one goal.
A mind free of any goal
Not quite. The article says: A single-focused mind fixed on one goal.
questions.rationale: “Super-achievement needs super endeavour done with a single-focused mind.”

questions.q: Molvi Lutfullah never attended an English school, yet wrote a book in English that was published in London. How did he learn the language?
options: By living in England for a decade
Not quite. The article says: By memorising ten words every night without fail for eight years.
By employing an English tutor
Not quite. The article says: By memorising ten words every night without fail for eight years.
By memorising ten words every night without fail for eight years
Well read. “Little by little becomes great.”
By translating Persian poetry
Not quite. The article says: By memorising ten words every night without fail for eight years.
questions.rationale: “During those eight years, not even a single night passed without having committed to memory ten words of the English language.”

questions.q: “Take care of the minutes, for the hours will take care of themselves.” What principle does the article draw from Lord Chesterfield’s advice?
options: Small things do not matter
Not quite. The article says: The whole is made of parts; great success is the sum of small ones.
Hours matter more than minutes
Not quite. The article says: The whole is made of parts; great success is the sum of small ones.
Time cannot really be saved
Not quite. The article says: The whole is made of parts; great success is the sum of small ones.
The whole is made of parts; great success is the sum of small ones
Correct. Five wasted minutes an hour add up to weeks.
questions.rationale: “Taking care of the parts is just as good as taking care of the whole… All great success ultimately boils down to an accumulation of small successes.”

questions.q: The article says experience teaches man two things about his position in the world. What are they?
options: That he is master of nature, and answerable to none
Not quite. The article says: That he is only a “taker,” and that there is another Being who is only a “giver”.
That he is unlucky, and others are fortunate
Not quite. The article says: That he is only a “taker,” and that there is another Being who is only a “giver”.
That he is alone, and must rely on himself
Not quite. The article says: That he is only a “taker,” and that there is another Being who is only a “giver”.
That he is only a “taker,” and that there is another Being who is only a “giver”
Yes. From this follows praise and thanks to God.
questions.rationale: “Experience shows man that in this world he is only a ‘taker’ and secondly that there is another Being Who is only a ‘giver’.”

questions.q: What does the article say makes a person able to speak soundly and straight?
options: A loud and confident voice
Not quite. The article says: Fear of God, which makes him sincere and honest so that his words match his thoughts.
A wide vocabulary
Not quite. The article says: Fear of God, which makes him sincere and honest so that his words match his thoughts.
Training in public speaking
Not quite. The article says: Fear of God, which makes him sincere and honest so that his words match his thoughts.
Fear of God, which makes him sincere and honest so that his words match his thoughts
Right. Such speech reaches people’s hearts.
questions.rationale: “Fear of God makes one highly sincere, responsible and honest. It is these qualities that makes one able to speak in a sound manner… There is no difference between his thinking and his speaking.”

questions.q: How does the article regard the discoveries of modern science?
options: As a threat to faith
Not quite. The article says: As uncovering the “words of God,” giving believers far more to reflect on.
As of use only to specialists
Not quite. The article says: As uncovering the “words of God,” giving believers far more to reflect on.
As uncovering the “words of God,” giving believers far more to reflect on
Yes. Science has widened the canvas of God-realisation.
As replacing the need for reflection
Not quite. The article says: As uncovering the “words of God,” giving believers far more to reflect on.
questions.rationale: “Modern science, in its reality, is another name for discovering these words of God… Now science has provided a huge library of unlimited data for the seekers of Ma’rifat.”

questions.q: According to the article, how does receiving in the next world differ from receiving in this one?
options: Here things are given as a test, deserved or not; there, only according to what one has earned
Exactly. Now is the time for action.
Here nothing is given; there everything is
Not quite. The article says: Here things are given as a test, deserved or not; there, only according to what one has earned.
Here the good are rewarded; there all are
Not quite. The article says: Here things are given as a test, deserved or not; there, only according to what one has earned.
There is no difference
Not quite. The article says: Here things are given as a test, deserved or not; there, only according to what one has earned.
questions.rationale: “In the world before death, man has been given a great number of things… whether or not he deserved them. But after death, the criterion of receiving will only be a matter of his just desserts.”

questions.q: A scientist said a day without a new discovery in nature felt wasted. What does the article say this means for a believer?
options: Faith should grow daily through fresh discovery of God; faith that does not grow is hardly faith
Well reasoned. God is a never-ending reality.
Believers should become scientists
Not quite. The article says: Faith should grow daily through fresh discovery of God; faith that does not grow is hardly faith.
Faith is complete once it is declared
Not quite. The article says: Faith should grow daily through fresh discovery of God; faith that does not grow is hardly faith.
Discovery belongs to science alone
Not quite. The article says: Faith should grow daily through fresh discovery of God; faith that does not grow is hardly faith.
questions.rationale: “Faith is another word for discovery of God… Faith that does not grow is not really faith at all.”
